question:
An 37-year-old male patient is evaluated for the onset of bright red blood per rectum. He denies
abdominal pain, and his past medical history is noncontributory. Vital signs are T 98°F, HR 100/min,
and blood pressure 127/81 mmHg. Abdominal exam is unremarkable, as is rectal exam. Which of the
following is the most likely cause of his presentation? Answer Choices: (A) Internal hemorrhoids (B)
Meckel’s diverticulum (C) Portal hypertensive gastropathy (D) Arteriovenous malformation (E)
Infectious colitis (F) Juvenile polyps (G) Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome (H) Inflammatory bowel disease
(I) Angiodysplasia (J) Chronic constipation with anal fissure

A. Chronic constipation with anal fissure
B. Portal hypertensive gastropathy
C. Inflammatory bowel disease
D. Meckel’s diverticulum
E. Angiodysplasia
F. Arteriovenous malformation
G. Juvenile polyps
H. Internal hemorrhoids
I. Infectious colitis
J. Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome
